In this notebook we will use the cNMF spectra identified using k=5,10,15,20,and 25 to generate metaprograms. 

## Set Up

```{r setup, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

# Set default ggplot theme
theme_set(
  theme_bw() +
    theme(
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", linewidth = 0.5)
    )
)

# some helpful settings
options(
  dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE, 
  readr.show_col_types = FALSE
)

set.seed(2025)
```

```{r}
# source in some helper functions we'll use to prep data 
# build_spectra_mtx() build_spectra_cor_df() filter_spectra()
source("./utils/spectra-helper-functions.R")
```

```{r}
# paths to custom geneset files we're going to use for GSEA and ORA
geneset_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "custom-gene-sets.tsv")
msigdb_geneset_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "msigdb-gene-sets.tsv")
category_file <- file.path("..", "genesets", "gene-set-categories.tsv")
```


```{r}
results_dir <- fs::path("..", "ews-nf-out", "cnmf")

# get all the spectra files
spectra_files <- fs::dir_ls(
  path = results_dir, 
  glob = "*.gene_spectra_score.k_*.dt_*.txt", 
  recurse = TRUE
  )

# extract the unique ID for labeling
unique_ids <- stringr::str_extract(spectra_files, pattern = "SCPCL[0-9]+-SCPCS[0-9]+")
names(spectra_files) <- unique_ids
```


## Generate Metaprograms

To generate the metaprograms (MPs), we're going to use three different sets of spectra from cNMF as input:

* `all`: All spectra from k=5,10,15,20, and 25
* `filtered`: Spectra after filtering redundant and orphan spectra 
* `small_k`: Spectra from k=5, 10, and 15 (no filtering of redundant or orphan)

```{r}
# read in and build spectra mtx
spectra_mtx <- build_spectra_mtx(spectra_files)

# get correlations
cor_matrix <- cor(spectra_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# creae correlation dataframe with info about each spectra
# we need this to help determine which spectra to filter
all_cor_df <- build_spectra_cor_df(cor_matrix)
```


```{r}
# get filtered spectra for all values of k 
discard_spectra <- filter_spectra(all_cor_df) |> 
  unlist()
filtered_spectra_mtx <- spectra_mtx[,!colnames(spectra_mtx) %in% discard_spectra]

# now just k = 5, 10, 15 
small_k_spectra <- colnames(spectra_mtx)[stringr::str_detect(colnames(spectra_mtx), "k05|k10|k15")]
small_k_spectra_mtx <- spectra_mtx[,small_k_spectra]
```

```{r}
# combine into a single list to use for getting MPs and evaluating metrics
mtx_list <- list(
  "all" = spectra_mtx,
  "filtered" = filtered_spectra_mtx,
  "small_k" = small_k_spectra_mtx
)
```

To get MPs, we'll use heirarchical clustering and cut the tree, specifying the value of k. 
For each cluster, we get the mean score of each gene across all spectra included in the cluster. 
If a gene is only found in some of the spectra, and therefore have `NA` values, the `NA` values will be ignored and the mean will only consider the spectra that have values. 

For each of the input sets of spectra, we'll get MPs using k=4, 6, and 12. 

```{r}
# get mps for each input 
# return list of clustered spectra, and mps
mp_results_list <- mtx_list |> 
  purrr::imap(\(mtx, strategy){
    
    # given the spectra mtx, calculate the correlation and then use hclust 
    cor_mtx <- cor(mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    dist_mtx <- as.dist(1-cor_mtx)
    tree <- hclust(dist_mtx, method = "ward.D2")

    # for each input, we will test multiple values of k
    k_values <- c(4,6,12)
    
    # for each k value generate the clusters and mps
    mp_list <- k_values |> 
      purrr::map(\(k) {
        clusters <- cutree(tree, k = k)
        mp_clusters <- split(colnames(mtx), clusters)
        
        # to get mps, take the mean of all genes across all spectra
        # and then sort by scores
        mps <- mp_clusters |>
          purrr::map(\(spectra_list){
            
            rowMeans(mtx[, spectra_list, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) |>
              sort(decreasing = TRUE)
            
          })
  
        names(mps) <- glue::glue("MP{names(mps)}")
        
        return(list(
          "clusters" = clusters,
          "metaprograms" = mps
        ))
        
      })
    
    names(mp_list) <- glue::glue("{strategy}-k{k_values}")
    
    return(mp_list)
  }) |> 
  unlist(recursive = FALSE)
names(mp_results_list) <- stringr::word(names(mp_results_list), -1, sep = "\\.")
```

### Other strategies for generating MPs 

Alternatively, we could first replace all `NA` values with zeros and then get the mean. 
I did this when initially looking at these results and saw similar results using the full set of cNMF spectra. 
I think we could explore this route to identify any differences, and if they are meaningful, but I felt that was outside the scope of this notebook, for now. 

I also looked at dropping genes that have `NA` values, which only left < 100 genes for each MP. 
The GSEA for those programs were all EMT/invasion/EWS pathways, with very little variation between MPs. 

## Evaluating MPs 

### Sample distribution

First, we will look at what percentage of the total samples are represented in each spectra. 


```{r}
clusters_df <- purrr::map_dfr(names(mp_results_list), \(strategy) {

  clusters_list <- mp_results_list[[strategy]]$clusters

  tibble::tibble(
    strategy = strategy,
    spectra = names(clusters_list),
    clusters = clusters_list
  )
}) |>
  # Extract sample ID before `_k_`
  dplyr::mutate(
    sample_id = stringr::word(spectra, 1, sep = "_") |> 
      stringr::word(-1, sep = "-"),
    metaprogram = glue::glue("MP{clusters}")
  ) 

# define the levels so k=12 is after k=6
strategy_levels <- names(mp_results_list)

freq_df <- clusters_df |> 
  dplyr::distinct(strategy, sample_id, metaprogram) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(strategy, metaprogram) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(n_samples = dplyr::n(),
                   pct_samples = 100 * (n_samples/13)) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(pct_samples)) |> 
  dplyr::ungroup() |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    metaprogram_levels = glue::glue("{strategy}-{metaprogram}"),
    metaprogram = factor(metaprogram_levels, levels = rev(metaprogram_levels)),
    y_labels = stringr::word(metaprogram, 1, sep = "-"),
    strategy = forcats::fct_relevel(strategy, strategy_levels)
  )
```


```{r, fig.height=8}
ggplot(freq_df, aes(x = pct_samples, y = metaprogram)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(strategy), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "% of samples",
    y = "Metaprogram",
  ) +
  theme_bw()

```

Not surprisingly, lower values of k have MPs that are found in all samples. 
As you increase k we get MPs that are found in only a subset of samples. 

### Correlation of MPs to each other

Here we look at the correlation of each MP to all other MPs. 
We want to get MPs that are unique to each other with low correlation to other MPs.
Note that part of why I chose k=12 is because that was the lowest value where most MPs were unique, but that doesn't mean they are all biologically meaningful. 

```{r}
mp_results_list |> 
  purrr::imap(\(results_list, strategy){
    
    # combine all mps into a matrix for a heatmap
    # get correlation to each other
    mp_mtx <- do.call(cbind, results_list$metaprograms)
    mp_cor_matrix <- cor(mp_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    
    ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
      mp_cor_matrix,
      column_title = strategy
    )
  })
```


### Correlation of MPs across filtering strategies {.tabset}

Now let's see how filtering might have affected MP identification. 
In particular, if we filter out redundant and orphan spectra and/or use a smaller value of K, how does that compare to using the full range of K in identifying MPs. 
Here we compare the MPs for each value of K between strategies. 

#### All vs. Filtered

```{r}
k_levels <- c("k4", "k6", "k12")
k_levels |> 
  purrr::map(\(k){
    
    # pull out mps for each condition
    all_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("all-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(all_mps) <- glue::glue("all-{names(all_mps)}")
    filtered_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("filtered-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(filtered_mps) <- glue::glue("filtered-{names(filtered_mps)}")
    
    # get mtx for each condition to compare
    all_mtx <- do.call(cbind, all_mps)
    filtered_mtx <- do.call(cbind, filtered_mps)
    
    mp_cor_matrix <- cor(all_mtx, filtered_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    
    ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
      mp_cor_matrix,
      column_title = k
    )
  })
```

#### All vs. Small values of K

```{r}
k_levels |> 
  purrr::map(\(k){
    
    all_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("all-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(all_mps) <- glue::glue("all-{names(all_mps)}")
    small_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("small_k-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(small_mps) <- glue::glue("small_k-{names(small_mps)}")
    
    all_mtx <- do.call(cbind, all_mps)
    small_mtx <- do.call(cbind, small_mps)
    
    mp_cor_matrix <- cor(all_mtx, small_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    
    ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
      mp_cor_matrix,
      column_title = k
    )
  })
```

#### Filtered vs. small values of K 

```{r}
k_levels |> 
  purrr::map(\(k){
    
    filtered_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("filtered-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(filtered_mps) <- glue::glue("filtered-{names(filtered_mps)}")
    small_mps <- mp_results_list[[glue::glue("small_k-{k}")]]$metaprograms
    names(small_mps) <- glue::glue("small_k-{names(small_mps)}")
    
    filtered_mtx <- do.call(cbind, filtered_mps)
    small_mtx <- do.call(cbind, small_mps)
    
    mp_cor_matrix <- cor(filtered_mtx, small_mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    
    ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
      mp_cor_matrix,
      column_title = k
    )
  })
```

It looks like we are getting different MPs when filtering or using small values of K compared to the full range. 
So maybe by keeping all those K, we are getting more programs that might just be noise? 
Interestingly, removing the redundant and orphan spectra is comparable to using a small range of K at least for lower values of MP clusters. 

### Alright so what are these genes? 

Let's look at the top 10 genes for each MP. 
I'm mainly looking for any easily distinguishable groups of genes, like ribosomal or cycling genes or obvious Ewing genes.  

```{r}
ensembl <- biomaRt::useEnsembl(biomart = "ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")
map_df <- biomaRt::getBM(
  attributes = c("ensembl_gene_id", "hgnc_symbol"),
  filters = "ensembl_gene_id",
  values = genes_df$gene_id,
  mart = ensembl
) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    gene_id = ensembl_gene_id,
    gene_name = hgnc_symbol
  )

genes_df <- purrr::map_dfr(names(mp_results_list), \(strategy) {

  mp_list <- mp_results_list[[strategy]]$metaprograms
  
  mp_list |> 
    purrr::imap_dfr(\(mp, mp_name){
      tibble::tibble(
        strategy = strategy,
        metaprogram = mp_name,
        gene_id = names(mp)[1:10],
      )
    })
}) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(map_df, by = "gene_id")

```

```{r}
split(genes_df, genes_df$strategy) |> 
  purrr::map(DT::datatable)
```

I'm not sure that this is super helpful at this point, but I do see some EWS high and low targets coming up. 

In the `all-k12` group, MP5 does have mostly heatshock proteins.
In the `small_k-k12` group, MP5 is also heatshock proteins.
I don't see this same group in the filtered group, so maybe that approach is helping us? 
Or maybe we're throwing out spectra that could help us identify a group of low quality cells?

### GSEA of metaprograms 

Now, we'll go GSEA of each of the MPs. 
We want to know what gene sets could be present and how unique the MPs are from each other. 

We'll use the EWS::FLI1 activated and repressed gene sets and the hallmarks gene sets from MSigDb. 
I expect to see some MP with enrichment of EWS activated and repressed gene sets, EMT gene sets, and proliferative gene sets.

```{r}
# read in custom gene lists and EF msigdb gene sets to look at 
geneset_df <- readr::read_tsv(geneset_file)
ef_msigdb_df <- readr::read_tsv(msigdb_geneset_file)

# use hallmarks in addition to EF lists 
hallmarks_msigdb_df <- msigdbr::msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name, ensembl_gene)
```

```{r}
# get list of categories that we need to grab from msigdb
category_list <- ef_msigdb_df |>
  dplyr::select(category, subcategory) |>
  unique() |>
  purrr::transpose()


# list of genesets and names
geneset_list <- ef_msigdb_df$geneset |>
  purrr::set_names(ef_msigdb_df$name)

# first pull out info for each category and then pull out specific genes for geneset
ef_geneset_df <- category_list |>
  purrr::map(\(category_list){
    # replace subcategory with default NULL
    # can't use NULL in tsv since it gets read in as a character
    if (is.na(category_list$subcategory)) {
      subcategory <- NULL
    } else {
      subcategory <- category_list$subcategory
    }
    
    msigdbr::msigdbr(
      species = "Homo sapiens",
      collection = category_list$category,
      subcollection = subcategory
    )
  }) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  # only keep relevant gene sets
  dplyr::filter(gs_name %in% geneset_list) |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name, ensembl_gene)

# combine into a single term2df for running GSEA and ORA
all_term_df <- geneset_df |> 
  dplyr::select(gs_name = geneset, ensembl_gene = ensembl_gene_id) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(ef_geneset_df) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(hallmarks_msigdb_df) |> 
  tidyr::drop_na()
```

```{r, warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
# get a new list of just mps from mp_results
mp_list <- mp_results_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(results_list) results_list$metaprograms)

# now run GSEA
gsea_results <- mp_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(mps){
    mps |> 
      purrr::map(\(genes){
        
        clusterProfiler::GSEA(
          geneList = genes,
          minGSSize = 25,
          TERM2GENE = all_term_df
        )
      })
  })

# combine gsea results into a dataframe
gsea_df <- gsea_results |> 
  purrr::map(\(results_list){
    results_list |> 
      purrr::imap_dfr(\(results, mp){
        results@result |> 
          dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(NES)) |> 
          dplyr::select(NES, pvalue, p.adjust) |> 
          dplyr::mutate(
            metaprogram = mp
          ) |> 
          tibble::rownames_to_column("geneset")
        
      })
  }) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "strategy") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(geneset = forcats::fct_reorder(geneset, NES, .desc = TRUE))
```

```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=15}
# plot the GSEA NES score for each gene set across each MP and each strategy 
split(gsea_df, gsea_df$strategy) |> 
  purrr::imap(\(df, strategy){
    # do some factor reordering to make sure the NES scores are ordered within each MP 
    df |> 
      dplyr::group_by(metaprogram, geneset) |> 
      dplyr::arrange(desc(NES)) |> 
      dplyr::ungroup() |> 
      dplyr::mutate(
        geneset_levels = glue::glue("{metaprogram}-{geneset}"),
        geneset = factor(geneset_levels, levels = rev(geneset_levels)),
        y_labels = stringr::word(geneset, 1, sep = "-")
      ) |> 
      ggplot(aes(x = NES, y = geneset)) +
      geom_col() +
      facet_wrap(vars(metaprogram), ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
      theme_bw() +
      labs(
        title = strategy
      )
    
  })
```

Honestly, this is a lot... 
There's definitely a trend of MPs having EWS activated and repressed targets. 
We need to look at this more closely to really annotate them, but I do think we are getting biologically distinct MPs at the higher values of k. 
The lower values of k really highlight the EF high and repressed states, which I would expect to be the main "cell states" in this dataset.

Let's also look at how unique each of the genesets are. 
The plot below counts how many times each geneset has a positive NES in MPs. 

```{r, fig.height=20, fig.width=15}
geneset_count_df <- gsea_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(NES > 0) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(strategy) |> 
  dplyr::count(geneset)

split(geneset_count_df, geneset_count_df$strategy) |> 
  purrr::imap(\(df, strategy){
    ggplot(df, aes(x = n, y = forcats::fct_reorder(geneset, n))) +
      geom_col() + 
      labs(title = strategy,
           y = "",
           x = "Number of MPs with geneset") 
    
  }) |> 
  patchwork::wrap_plots(ncol = 2)
```

### ORA 

Finally, we'll do some ORA with just the top 200 genes in each MP. 

```{r}
# get the universe of HVGs across all input samples
universe <- rownames(spectra_mtx)

ora_results <- mp_list |> 
  purrr::map(\(results){
    results |> 
      purrr::map(\(scores){
        genes <- names(scores)[1:200]
        
        ora_results <- clusterProfiler::enricher(
          gene = genes,
          universe = universe,
          TERM2GENE = all_term_df
        )
      })

  })
```


```{r, fig.height=15, fig.width=15}
ora_results|> 
  purrr::imap(\(results_list, strategy){
    results_list |> 
      purrr::imap(\(result, mp){
        if(nrow(result) > 0) {
          enrichplot::dotplot(result, title = mp)
        }
      }) |> 
      purrr::compact() |>
      patchwork::wrap_plots(ncol = 2) +
      patchwork::plot_annotation(title = strategy)
  })
```

## Conclusions

This is a lot, but I do think we are generating MPs that might be meaningful. 
We are seeing a lot of programs that I would expect, like EF activated and repressed gene sets, EMT gene sets, etc. 
More careful curation of the genesets and GSEA/ORA results are needed to actually annotate them, but I think we are getting some unique MPs even at the higher values of k. 

It seems like filtering and small k give similar spectra to each other, but when k goes up to 12 we don't see as much similarity. 
It could be helpful to look specifically at the MPs that are different and the same in those two groups to see what we gain/lose by filtering vs. just using a smaller k.
